康加鼓以手指與手掌擊打鼓面發聲。初學可先坐著演奏，或將鼓置於架子上站立演奏。基本: The conga sounds when struck with the fingers and palms on the head. A beginner can play seated, or with the drum on a stand while standing. The basic sequence is: first strike an open tone near the rim with the four fingers, then muffle the sound by laying the fingers on the head, or play a bass tone with a slightly cupped palm away from the centre; the slap is harder and needs a clear bounce. When tuning, the tension around the head must be even: too slack and the bass and slap sound dull, too tight and the sound is unnatural.
康加鼓可從非洲裔古巴音樂的康加與倫巴場合聆聽，早期每位鼓手只擊一鼓；二十世紀中葉: The conga can be heard in the conga and rumba settings of Afro-Cuban music, where early on each drummer played a single drum; after the mid-twentieth century one player often plays two or three drums at once. It also appears in Cuban son ensembles, in descarga, Afro-Cuban jazz, cha-cha-chá, songo, merengue and Latin rock. In Cuba and Latin America it is mostly played by hand; in Trinidadian calypso and soca it is sometimes struck with sticks, and in the Congo region one hand and one stick is common. The conga is also used in the rumba and comparsa ensembles of large drum groups, or to fill out the rhythm section in other ensembles.
康加鼓為單面膜鳴鼓，以手指與手掌擊打。開放音清晰共鳴，悶音因手指貼住鼓面而短促，: The conga is a single-headed membranophone struck with the fingers and palms. The open tone rings clearly, the muted tone is short because the fingers rest on the head, the bass tone is struck with the whole palm and is deep, and the slap is loud with a sharp crack. Range changes with the diameter of the head: a large head is lower and a small head higher, so the quinto is highest, the tres dos in the middle and the tumba lowest. Tuning adjusts the head tension with screws; too slack makes the bass and slap dull, too tight makes them thin and narrow, and head tension also affects bounce and volume.
康加鼓起源不詳，研究者認為由古巴非裔族群於十九世紀末或二十世紀初發展，祖先可能為: The origin of the conga is unknown; researchers hold that it was developed by Cubans of African descent in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, with ancestors possibly among the Bantu yuka and makuta and the Yoruba bembe drums. It was used early in Cuban music and rumba, one drum per player. After the mid-twentieth century, innovations in playing and construction and its international spread made two or three drums common, and it entered Latin music. The word "conga" became widespread in the 1930s as Latin music became popular in the United States, coming from the carnival rhythm la conga; the screw tension system appeared in the 1950s.

The conga (also called tumbadora) is a tall, narrow Cuban barrel drum with a single head, a membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.221.1. The modern body is mostly wood or fibreglass, tuned with screws. The drummer strikes it with fingers and palms; in traditional Afro-Cuban music one player had one drum, and later two to four drums are often grouped; in Cuba and Latin America it is mostly played by hand, while in Trinidadian calypso and soca drumsticks are sometimes used. Drummers use it in rumba, conga, son and salsa settings.
現代康加鼓琴身多以木板條拼成桶狀，或使用玻璃纖維；鼓面以螺絲張力系統固定。鼓面材: The body of the modern conga is mostly built from wooden staves into a barrel shape, or of fibreglass; the head is fixed by a screw tension system. The head material and the other parts are not stated. Early instruments were tuned with knots and tension ropes, or by heating the nailed head; the modern tension system uses screws and lugs.
